Title: Non‐Substituted Aromatic Pyridine N‐Oxide Additives with an Intrinsic N→O Acceptor for Ultra‐Long‐Life Zn||MnO2 Batteries
Text:
Zinc-Ion Batteries
Non-Substituted Aromatic Pyridine N-Oxide Additives with an
Intrinsic N!O Acceptor for Ultra-Long-Life Znj jMnO2 Batteries
Qin Kang, Hongyu Liang,* Zhaomin Zhu, Fuxu Xing, Bingzheng Zhu, Yuman Li,
Shihao Wang, Shengda Tang, Hui Li, Li Pan, Lijun Yang, Tangming Mo,* and
Yongfeng Bu*
Abstract: Various organic and inorganic reagents con-
taining N/O functional groups have been developed as
additives to aqueous electrolytes (e.g., ZnSO4, ZS) of
zinc-ion batteries (ZIBs). However, finding an additive
that can significantly enhance the durability of Zn
anodes by inhibiting Zn dendrites and side reactions
remains a considerable challenge. Herein, pyridine N-
oxide (PNO), a non-substituted aromatic compound
with a nitrogen positive charge-induced N!O bond, is
explored as ZS additives for highly durable Zn plating/
stripping electrolytes (i.e., PNO/ZS). The optimized
PNO0.03/ZS mixture demonstrates exceptional stability
for Zn anodes, achieving a cycle life exceeding 4200 h
and a Coulombic efficiency of 99.9% at 1 mAcm� 2 and
1 mAhcm� 2. It maintains over 1000 h of life and a
cumulative capacity of 2.5 Ahcm� 2, even when subjected
to plating/stripping conditions intensified by a factor of
5. Importantly, it enables Znj jα-MnO2 cells to sustain
high-current
charge/discharge
cycles
for
over
5000
cycles,
retaining
80%
(125 mAhg� 1)
of
the
initial
capacity, which is the best performance reported for
similar additive systems. This exceptional stability is
ascribed to the highly reversible Zn anode plating/
stripping, facilitated by the suitable coordination inter-
actions between the N!O acceptor of PNO and the
Zn2+/H2O donor, effectively inhibiting side reactions.
1. Introduction
Aqueous batteries are ideal for large-scale electrical energy
storage due to their low cost, high safety, and environmental
compatibility, aligning with sustainable development goals
based on renewable energy. Compared to other ion batteries
(e.g., Li+, Na+, K+),[1–4] aqueous zinc ion batteries (ZIBs)
offer cost-effective performance owing to their high specific
capacity (820 mAhg� 1) and low Zn2+/Zn redox potential
(� 0.76 V vs. SHE).[5–7] However, drawbacks caused by
typical ZnSO4 (ZS) aqueous electrolytes, such as Zn anode
dendrite growth and H2O side reactions (e.g., H2 evolution
and corrosion), had greatly restricted the cycle life and
stability of ZIBs. The dendrite is due to uneven charge
distribution during Zn plating/stripping,[8] while the side
reactions involve highly reactive H2O at the Zn/electrolyte
interface, leading to the formation of compounds like
Znx(OH)y(SO4)z
2+/1+/ZnO/Zn(OH)2,
which
reduce
Zn
anode utilization.[9] Developing Zn anode protection strat-
egies has become a focus for ZIBs, including Zn anode
modifications,[10,11] separator coatings,[12,13] and electrolyte
additives.[5,14,15]
The
tactic
of
electrolyte
additives
are
regarded as particularly promising due to their simplicity,
efficiency,
and
compatibility
with
conventional
battery
manufacturing.
Typical electrolyte additives for ZIBs include organic
molecules[16,17] and inorganic/organic salts[18–20] (e.g., ionic
liquids[21]) additives that contain N/O-related hydrophilic
functional groups. Compared to organic small molecules,
organic macromolecules not only suppress dendrite growth
by regulating Zn2+
cluster structures in ZS but also
contribute to the modulation of the Zn anode surface
through their flexible long-chain/host-guest structures;[9,15]
their functional group dissociation is usually low except for
strong organic acids/amines. Inorganic/organic salt additives
in ZS are highly dissociated into polar anions (e.g., � COO� )
and cations (e.g., Mg2+),[18,22] which inhibit Zn dendrite
growth by shielding Zn surface tips or compensating electro-
lyte carriers. These ions are in a strongly polarized state and
may interact strongly with charged Zn2+ species. Effective
Zn anode plating/stripping in ZS requires appropriate Zn2+
desolvation and solvation energies. Thus, H-bond acceptors
in electrolyte additives with suitable coordination to Zn2+ or
Zn are essential for a reversible and fast Zn plating/stripping
process. The ideal additive should inhibit Zn dendrites and
H2O electrochemical activity within the inner Helmholtz

In this study, we report that non-substituted aromatic
pyridine N-oxide (PNO), featuring an un-ionized, polar-
appropriate N!O acceptor induced by a positively charged
N center, acts as a highly efficient additive for ZS electro-
lytes in ZIBs. PNO harbors an N!O coordination bond,
distinct from other organic molecules or salt additives. The
coordination ability of the N!O acceptor with donors (e.g.,
Zn2+/H2O) in the modified H-bonding network lies theoret-
ically between that of organic molecules and ionic acceptors,
allowing Zn2+
to achieve suitable desolvation/solvation
energies for uniform plating/stripping of Zn anodes while
suppressing H2O activity in IHP.[23] As a result, Znj jZn cells
with the optimized PNO0.03/ZS electrolyte exhibit excep-
tional cycling stability (up to 4200 h at 1 mAcm� 2 and
1 mAhcm� 2) and a Coulombic efficiency (CE) of 99.9%;
even under deep plating/stripping conditions (5 mAcm� 2
and 5 mAhcm� 2), the stability extends up to 1000 h. The
remarkable cycling performance of Znj jα-MnO2 cells fur-
ther underscores the advantages of PNO in stabilizing the
highly reversible plating/stripping of Zn anodes, achieving
80% capacity retention after 5000 cycles at a high current
density (5 Ag� 1), far surpassing other reported aromatic
heterocyclic additives in both cell life and capacity retention.

the
tremendous
potential
of
PNO
application in ZS electrolytes for ZIBs.

2.2. Reconfiguration of IHP by PNO
Figure 2 presents theoretical and experimental results of the
effect of PNO on the IHP at the Zn anode. The adsorption
energy of PNO on Zn (002) is significantly higher than that
of H2O (� 0.078 eV, Figure 2a), with PNO favoring vertical
adsorption (v-PNO) over horizontal adsorption (h-PNO)
due
to
the
higher
adsorption
energy
(� 0.213 eV
vs.
� 0.097 eV, Figure S4). Relative to h-PNO and H2O, there is
a stronger electronic interaction/charge transfer between Zn
(002) and the O of the strongly polarized N!O bond of the
v-PNO, which is likely due to electron cloud overlap, as
shown in the 3D charge density difference and the corre-
sponding 2D slice diagram (Figure 2b). The preferential
adsorption of PNO on Zn (002) is further corroborated by
its higher HOMO energy level (� 4.2 eV) compared to H2O
(� 7.1 eV, Figure 2c), and by the reduction in electrical
double layer capacitance induced by PNO adsorption (42.8
vs. 126.1 μF cm� 2, Figure S5). Theoretical simulations in-
dicate that PNO, when adsorbed on the Zn anode surface,
reconfigures the IHP, forming an H2O-depleted electrode
interface in the electrical double layer (Figure 2d).[20]
More experimental data about specific adsorption of
PNO on the surface of Zn foil is obtained using spectro-
scopic techniques. For example, Raman spectra of Zn
soaked in PNO0.03/H2O solution show characteristic signals
of in-plane ring bending and ring stretching/C� H bending of
PNO at 640, 1024, and 1190 cm� 1, respectively, confirming
that PNO is indeed adsorbed on the surface (Figure 2e,
Figure S6). In contrast, the Zn soaked in H2O shows no such
signals; instead, a significant Zn� O signal was observed at
437 cm� 1.[38] This Zn� O signal is minimal if Zn is soaked in
PNO0.03/H2O solution, lending further support that the
adsorbed PNO may effectively inhibit the side reactions of
Zn with H2O. It is also supported by FTIR spectra data
(Figure S7a). The N� C and N� H/N+ signals of PNO are
also detected in the XPS fine spectra of N 1s, confirming
that PNO in H2O spontaneously adsorbs on the Zn foil
surface (Figure 2f). The C� N peak (287.8 eV) on the Zn
surface after 10 cycles shifts right by 1.3 eV compared to the
one
soaked
in
PNO0.03/H2O
(286.5 eV)
(Figures S7b,c),
suggesting that the fresh surface formed by Zn plating/
stripping adsorbs PNO and alters the chemical environment

2.3. Suppression of Zn Dendrites by PNO
Figure 3 displays the nucleation growth of Zn plating in
PNO0.03/ZS electrolyte. Optical microscopy coupled with in
situ Raman spectroscopy monitors the Zn morphology and
electrolyte changes near the solid-liquid interface as a
function of the plating time. In ZS electrolyte, distinct
worm-like micro-protrusions appear on the Zn surface at
10 min, pronouncing at 20 and 30 min (Figure 3a). In
contrast, Zn in PNO0.03/ZS electrolyte shows almost no
surface protrusions throughout the 0-30 min plating process
(Figure 3a’). In situ Raman results show that the SO4
2�signal (~980 cm� 1) near the Zn/PNO0.03/ZS interface remains
constant during plating (right of Figure 3b), whereas in ZS
electrolyte, it rapidly decays after ~10 min and disappears
entirely by ~37 min due to concentration polarization (left
of Figure 3b).[44,45] The Raman signal at 980 cm� 1 represents
the change in Zn2+ concentration at the interface.[45] The
plating layer gradually moves along the Zn/electrolyte inter-
face during the Zn plating, so the Zn2+ concentration change
reflects the electric field‘s uniformity during the plating
reaction. In ZS
electrolyte, the
rapid decay
of Zn2+
concentration near the interface is detrimental to the
uniformity of Zn plating, while in PNO0.03/ZS electrolyte,
the homogeneous Zn2+ distribution reduces the develop-
ment of an inhomogeneous electric field, resulting in a non-
dendritic and highly reversible Zn plating reaction. Similar
behavior is observed during Zn stripping, indicating that

PNO adsorbed on the Zn surface enhances the uniform
Zn2+
concentration distribution during plating/stripping.
The overpotential for Zn2+ electroplating nucleation in
PNO0.03/ZS (39.7 mV) is notably higher than in ZS solution
(35.3 mV), supporting the effectiveness of PNO in suppress-
ing Zn dendrite growth (Figure 3c). Zn2+ migration in
PNO0.03/ZS electrolyte is dominated by faster 3D diffusion
(200 s) compared to slower 2D diffusion (800 s) in ZS
solution (inset of Figure 3c), corroborating the optical
observations of a more homogeneous and denser plating
nucleation in PNO0.03/ZS electrolyte.[37,46]
Symmetric Znj jZn cells are employed to simulate the
plating/stripping performance of Zn anodes in PNO0.03/ZS
electrolyte.[47] After 10 cycles at elevated plating/stripping
conditions (5 mAcm� 2, 5 mAhcm� 2), the surfaces of Zn
anodes in PNO0.03/ZS display typical Zn (002) features,
characterized by a relatively flat, dendrite-free hexagonal
texture (right side of Figure 3d). The corresponding UTM
also shows smaller height fluctuations of 0-10 μm (left side
of Figure 3d). In contrast, Zn anodes in ZS under the same
conditions exhibit disorganized micrometer-sized dendrites
instead of the typical hexagonal texture (Figures S8c,d),
whose height fluctuations in the UTM are amounted to 0-
39 μm. This suggests that PNO effectively protects Zn from
side reactions with H2O. The Tafel curve in Figure 3e shows
that Zn in PNO0.03/ZS has a lower corrosion current (0.013
vs. 0.022 mAcm� 2) and a higher corrosion voltage (16.5 vs.
� 23.1 mV) compared to ZS,[48,49] proving that PNO effec-
tively inhibits corrosion reactions of Zn surface. The H2O-
poor IHP environment induced by PNO adsorption on Zn
suppresses the electrochemical reduction activity of H2O, as
evidenced by an increase of up to 73 mV in the H2 evolution
potential (Figure 3f).[50] XRD results show that the inter-
facial layer after cycling in PNO0.03/ZS is virtually free of
unfavorable Zn4SO4(OH)6 5H2O at 8.4 degrees and ZnO at
33.8 degrees (Figure S10), suggesting PNO suppresses side
reactions on the Zn anode. The corresponding TEM image
reveals that the interfacial layer has an amorphous structure
of ~10 nm thickness on the Zn surface (Figure 3g), with the
exposed surface mainly Zn (002) based on its 0.24 nm
spacing in the enlarged image. With the Ar+ etching time
increases from 50 to 150 s, the XPS signals of the interfacial
layer, including C=C/C� C and O-C=O of C 1s and O� C and
O� Zn of O 1s, gradually decrease (Figure 3h), while C� N
signals on the surface before etching are hardly detected,
indicating PNO is mainly concentrated on the surface
adsorption layer. However, O-C=O and O� Zn signals from
ZnCO3 and ZnO persist during etching,[51] implying their
involvement in the interfacial layer formation. As expected,
the proportion of Zn2+ in the Zn 2p signal from ZnCO3/
ZnO decreases while Zn0 increases (Figure 3i). Depth
profiling XPS spectra analysis unravels that the interfacial
layer in PNO0.03/ZS consists of PNO or organic compounds
as the outer layer, and ZnCO3 and ZnO as the inner layer.
As a result, PNO with a strongly polar N!O acceptor not
only inhibits the growth of Zn dendrites by modulating
active H2O within the IHP but also reduces side reactions of
H2 evolution and corrosion through the in situ formation of
the interfacial layer, enhancing the long-range dendrite-free
plating/stripping process with a Zn (002) dominated growth
mechanism.
2.4. High Stability Conferred by Reversible Zn Plating/Stripping
in PNO/ZS

Znj jZn cells using PNO/ZS electrolyte, as well as the CE
performance of the corresponding Znj jCu cells. The PNO
content in ZS electrolyte is optimized by monitoring the
plating/stripping cycle life of Znj jZn cells with various
PNO
concentrations
under
fast
testing
conditions
(5 mAcm� 2, 5 mAhcm� 2). Notably, the cells using PNO0.03/
ZS exhibit the longest cycle life of over 1000 h, compared to
95 h for ZS, 712 h for PNO0.01/ZS, and 451 h for PNO0.05/ZS
(Figure S11a).
Corresponding
Znj jCu
cells
exhibit
an
average CE of over 99.6%, which is superior to ZS (98.4%)
under the same conditions (1 mAcm� 2, 1 mAhcm� 2) (Fig-
ure S11b). Remarkably, the Znj jCu cell with PNO0.03/ZS
electrolyte maintains a CE of 99.6% even after 1200 h of
plating/stripping
under
more
stringent
conditions
(10 mAcm� 2, 1 mAhcm� 2). It is interesting to note that a
very low amount (<0.03 molL� 1) of PNO is detrimental to
the improvement of plating/stripping stability and CE, while
too much PNO (>0.03 molL� 1) leads to reduced cycle life
due
to
increased
polarization
and

3. Conclusions
In summary, this study demonstrates that non-substituted
aromatic PNO, containing a polar N!O coordination bond,
are highly effective additives for improving the performance
of ZS in ZIBs. The optimal concentration of PNO in ZS was
determined to be 0.03 molL� 1. The positively charged N
enhances the electronegativity of the O in the N!O bond,
promoting PNO adsorption on the Zn anode surface in a
vertical manner. This reconfigures the IHP layer, reducing
the reactive H2O molecules at the interface. The polarity-
appropriate N!O bond in the studied PNO additives also
acts as an H-bond acceptor, forming reconfigured H-bond
networks that modulate the solvation structure of Zn2+ ions
in the ZS solution, thereby suppressing dendrite growth and
side reactions during the Zn plating/stripping processes. The
content-optimized PNO enables the Zn anode to achieve a
stable lifetime of up to 4200 h with a CE of 99.9% and
1000 h under more demanding conditions, significantly out-
performing other aromatic N-heterocyclic additives. Fur-
thermore, ZIBs using PNO can undergo >5000 cycles at
5 Ag� 1 with >80% capacity retention, representing one of
the longest lifetimes for batteries using MnO2 as the cathode
materials. The efficient PNO additive strategy, leveraging
the positively charged N centers to modulate the IHP layer
via a N!O acceptor and achieve dendrite-free Zn plating/
stripping, offers a promising approach for advancing the
commercialization of ZIBs.

Abstract: Various organic and inorganic reagents con- taining N/O functional groups have been developed as additives to aqueous electrolytes (e.g., ZnSO4, ZS) of zinc-ion batteries (ZIBs). However, finding an additive that can significantly enhance the durability of Zn anodes by inhibiting Zn dendrites and side reactions remains a considerable challenge. Herein, pyridine N- oxide (PNO), a non-substituted aromatic compound with a nitrogen positive charge-induced N!O bond, is explored as ZS additives for highly durable Zn plating/ stripping electrolytes (i.e., PNO/ZS).
